lesson.title: Steps a machine could follow

steps.headline: Steps with nothing left to guess

lead.text: Start with a card a machine could follow. Here is one: start with 8, add 4, halve what you have. Anyone who follows it ends up with 6. Nobody has to decide anything, because every step says exactly what to do and the steps come in a fixed order.

A card like that is an algorithm, a finite list of exact steps that ends with an answer. Finite means the list runs out. Exact means that no step leaves a choice open, so “add 4” counts and “add a bit” does not. A computer can follow only instructions that pass that test, which is why the first job in programming is to turn something you know how to do into steps that exact.
Notice that you also kept a running number in your head while you followed the card: 8, then 12, then 6. A program needs somewhere to keep that number too, and the next screen shows where.

diagram.alt: A card of three instructions: start with 8, add 4, halve it. Below it a box shows the running number after the chosen step: 8, then 12, then 6.
diagram.caption: Each step works on the number the step before left. Use the buttons to move down the card.

lead.text: Here is another card. Follow it in the order written and keep the running number in your head.

reveal.text: You held 10, then 6, then 3. Each step worked on the number the step before had left.

steps.headline: A named place for the number

lead.text: A program keeps its running number in a variable, which is a named box that holds one value at a time. The name used in these lessons is x. Putting a value into the box is called assignment, and it is written with an equals sign.

The line x = 3 means “store 3 in x”. The line x = x + 2 looks odd if you remember equals from school, because no number is equal to itself plus 2. In a program the sign means store, and the line works in two moves. The machine first works out the right-hand side using whatever x holds right now. Then it stores the answer back in x.

afterFigure.text: Press Run code under the picture and move through the trace. After the first line the box holds 3. The second line reads that 3, adds 2 and stores 5. The 3 has gone, because the box holds one value at a time.
One line is easy to follow. A program has many, so the next question is which one the machine takes first.

lead.text: Think back to the second line of the last picture.

A program is a list of lines, and the machine runs them from the top, one at a time. Each line sees the box as the line before left it. Nothing runs ahead of its turn, and nothing runs twice unless a later lesson says it should.
That gives a simple way to follow any program by hand, which is called tracing. Write down what the box holds after each line, and use the newest figure for the next line.

afterFigure.text: In the picture x starts at 2. The second line adds 6, so the box holds 8. The third line doubles it, so the box holds 16. The doubling worked on 8 because 8 was what the line above had left. The 2 had already been replaced.
Tracing is the skill the rest of the course relies on. Try it on a program of your own.

lead.text: Write down the value of x after each line, and use the newest value for the next line.

reveal.text: You carried one value down the lines: 3, then 5, then 20. Each line used what the line above left behind.

steps.headline: The same lines in a different order

lead.text: The order of the lines is part of the program. Take two instructions, double x and add 1, with x starting at 5. Doubling first gives 10, so adding 1 afterwards gives 11. Adding 1 first gives 6, so doubling afterwards gives 12. Two different answers came from the same two instructions.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows both orders, one on each button. Each instruction works on whatever the one before it left, so swapping two of them changes what each has to work with. An algorithm is a list of exact steps, and the order is one of the things it has to be exact about.
Now try a pair where you can check the effect for yourself.

steps.headline: Run x = 3, then x = x * 4, then x = x + 2. What is the final x?

workedSteps.text: Line 3 adds 2 to what x holds now.

steps.headline: A new value replaces the old one

lead.text: So far each line after the first has used the old value of x in its sum. That is common, and it is not required. A line such as x = 1 does not read x at all. It puts 1 in the box and throws away whatever was there.

Take a program that stores 9, then stores 1, then adds 5. The first line puts 9 in the box. The second replaces it with 1, so the 9 is gone for good. The third line reads the box, finds 1 and stores 6. Nothing in the program remembers the 9, unless an earlier line had copied it somewhere else.

afterFigure.text: That is the second thing a trace has to follow. A line can read the box, and a line can overwrite it. When you trace a program, cross out the old value each time a new one is stored, so that you never use a figure that has already been replaced.

steps.headline: Find x at the end of x = 2, then x = x + 3, then x = x * 5.

workedSteps.text: Line 2 reads x, adds 3 and stores the result.
Line 3 reads the new x and multiplies it.

lead.text: Decide which line stores a value without reading x, then carry on to the end.

reveal.text: The 7 was replaced on line 2, so line 3 never saw it. A replaced value is gone unless the program keeps it elsewhere.

lead.text: A procedure should add 1 to its input, then triple the result. This version has a slip in its last line: it adds 3 instead.

reveal.text: Repairing means finding the line that breaks the plan and then tracing again. You traced 4, then 5, then 15.

lesson.orientation: Trace a short program line by line, and see why the order of its instructions matters.
lesson.nextAction: Trace a procedure containing a test, and predict which branch runs for given inputs.

blocks.text: Ask a friend to make you a cup of tea and you can leave a lot unsaid. “Not too strong, with a splash of milk” is enough, because your friend knows what too strong looks like and how big a splash is. They fill in whatever you leave out.

A computer fills in nothing. It does exactly what each line says, in the order the lines are written. It has no idea what you meant, so a phrase like “a splash of milk” leaves it stuck, because it cannot decide how much a splash is. To get a machine to do a job you have to write the job down so exactly that nobody needs any judgement to carry it out.
This lesson follows one number through a short program, one line at a time. Along the way you'll see what a line like x = x + 2 does and what happens when two lines swap places.

intro.promise: By the end you'll trace a short program line by line and say why swapping two instructions changes the answer.

recap.keyIdea: A program runs one instruction at a time. Each line works on the value the line above left in x, and a new assignment replaces the old value.

blocks.text: Back at the friend with the tea, a machine needs every step written down exactly. You followed a number through a program as 3, then 5, then 20. You ran the same two instructions the other way round and reached 14. You saw 7 replaced by 2 before it could be doubled, and you mended a program until it finished at 15.

recap.nextHook: Every line so far has run, whatever x held. The next lesson opens with a café that takes £4 off a bill only when it is over £30, which is a line that looks at a value before it decides.

questions.prompt: Follow the three lines in order. What is x when the program ends?
hints: Follow the original program from top to bottom.
Start at 3, apply the addition, then apply multiplication to the updated value.
Do not apply both operations to the original 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Starting at 3, adding 2 gives 5, then multiplying by 4 gives 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. Each line works on the value the line above left in x: 3, then 5, then 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.
That multiplies first and adds second. Run the lines top to bottom, as written.
Line 3 multiplies what line 2 stored, not the original 3.

questions.prompt: What is x once line 3 has run?
hints: The multiplication now runs before the addition.
First calculate 3 × 4.
Use that updated value in the final +2 step.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Multiplying 3 by 4 gives 12, then adding 2 gives 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. The same two instructions in the other order give a different answer: each works on the value before it.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 first, then multiplies. Here the multiplication runs first.
That multiplies by 4 + 2. Line 3 adds 2 to the value line 2 stored.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to add 2.

questions.prompt: Run the three lines. What is x at the end?
hints: An assignment replaces the old value of x.
The line x = 2 overwrites the earlier 7.
Apply the final doubling to the newly stored value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second line replaces 7 with 2; doubling 2 gives 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The second line replaced 7 with 2, so only 2 reaches the doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the 7. Line 2 replaced it before line 3 ran.
Line 2 stores 2. It does not add 2 to the 7.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.

questions.prompt: Mend the last line so it triples x. Starting at x = 4, what does the repaired program finish with?
hints: Use the plan described above the program.
Start at 4, add 1, then multiply the updated value by 3.
Trace the repaired program, not the broken one.
questions.onCorrect: 15. Tracing the repaired program shows the plan working: add 1 first, then triple the result.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the broken version, which adds 3 to the updated x. The repair multiplies.
That triples first and adds 1 second. The plan adds 1 first.
That triples the 4 and skips the add. The plan adds 1 first.

questions.prompt: Trace x = 5, then x = x − 2, then x = x * 3. What is final x?
hints: Each assignment uses the value stored by the preceding line.
First update 5 by subtracting 2.
Multiply that new value by 3.
questions.onCorrect: 9. Each line works on the value the one before left: 5, then 3, then 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies before subtracting. Run the lines top to bottom.
That is x after line 2. Line 3 still has to run.

questions.prompt: Which instruction stores a precise new value?
hints: A machine instruction must say exactly how to update the stored value.
Look for an assignment with a defined arithmetic operation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The assignment x = x + 1 computes a new value from the current x and stores it. It gives a precise update the machine can execute.

questions.onCorrect: x = x + 1 is exact: it reads the current x, adds 1 and stores the result. A machine can follow it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Nicer” says nothing a machine could do. It needs an exact operation on x.
“A bit” is not an amount. A machine needs the exact change to make.

questions.prompt: A card says: start with 10, subtract 4, halve what you have. Follow it in the order written. What do you finish with?
hints: Do the first instruction only. What are you holding after it?
Now halve what you are holding, not the 10.
Half of 6.
questions.onCorrect: 3. You followed each instruction on the result of the one before. A program does exactly that, line by line.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves first. The instructions run in the order written, each on what the one before left.
That halves only the 4. The last instruction applies to everything you are holding.

questions.prompt: Why does line 3 multiply 5 and not 2?
hints: Which value is in x when line 3 starts?

acceptedIdeas: Line 2 replaced the 2 with 5, and line 3 reads what is stored now.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Line 2 replaced the 2 with 5, and line 3 reads what is stored now.

choices.label: Line 2 replaced the 2 with 5, and line 3 reads what is stored now.
Multiplication always uses the largest number the program has seen.
Line 3 uses the 3 from the line above it.

questions.onCorrect: The box holds one value at a time. Each assignment replaces it, and the next line reads the replacement.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in a program picks the largest value. A line reads whatever x holds when it runs.
The 3 was added to x on line 2. Line 3 reads x itself, which now holds the result.

hints: The equals sign in an assignment means store, so what does the line do to x?

acceptedIdeas: Reads x, adds 2 and stores the result in x.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reads x, adds 2 and stores the result in x.

choices.label: Reads x, adds 2 and stores the result in x.

questions.onCorrect: The right side is worked out from the current x, then stored back as x's new value.

misconceptions.feedback: As a statement of equality it could never be true. In a program the equals sign means store.
A comparison asks a question. This line changes x.

questions.prompt: A program starts with x = 6, adds 1, then doubles x. What does x finish as if the two instructions swap places?
hints: Which instruction now runs first?
Double the 6 before anything else.
Now add 1 to what you have.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Doubling first gives 12, then adding 1 gives 13.

questions.onCorrect: 13. Swapping two instructions changes what each one works on, so it changes the result.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original order. Here the doubling runs first.
That is the add on its own. The doubling still runs, and it runs first.
